eVisas

If you are granted protection status or permission to stay in the UK, and you have a valid passport or a biometric residence permit (BRP) that expired no later than 24 months or until 31 December 2026, whichever is sooner, the Home Office will automatically create a UKVI account for you and tell you how to access it. If this does not apply, you may be asked to create your own account after you receive a successful decision on your application.

Your UKVI account gives you access to a digital record of your immigration status, known as an eVisa. Your decision letter explains how you can create your UKVI account and sign in to access your eVisa.

An email address is required for your UKVI account. If you do not already have one, you should make arrangements to create one before creating your account, or if your account has been created for you and you do not have an email address, the UKVI Resolution Centre can support you in accessing your account. Contact UK Visas and Immigration for help - GOV.UK.

Contact UKVI by phone:

UK Visas and Immigration contact centre

Telephone: 0300 790 6268 - select option 2

Monday to Thursday (excluding bank holidays), 9am to 4:45pm

Friday (excluding bank holidays), 9am to 4:30pm Find out about call charges

If you were previously in the UK on another route, you may already have a UKVI account, and your eVisa will be linked to your existing account if you are granted permission to stay in the UK.

In the case of children, the expectation is that their parent or guardian will create and have access to their UKVI account and use the online services on their behalf. They can subsequently transfer ownership of the account and access to the online services to their child, usually when the child turns 18.

The Home Office is engaging with local authorities to ensure that they fulfil all their obligations to children in their care and care leavers with regards to creating a UKVI account and accessing their eVisa and proving their rights in the UK. The Local Authority can act as a proxy and support a child who is in their care by creating a UKVI account to access the child’s eVisa. When the person leaves care, the proxy can transfer the access back to the status holder.

Further information on the ‘helper’ and ‘proxy’ roles in managing a UKVI account can be found in the UKVI account: terms and conditions.

Once you access your UKVI account, you will be able to view the details of your eVisa online, for example your type of permission to stay, when it expires and your conditions of stay. You will also be able to update your personal details and register your passport, if applicable, in your UKVI account so that you can easily travel to and from the UK. Guidance on using your eVisa can be found at the following link: eVisas: access and use your online immigration status: What an eVisa is

If you need to provide evidence of your permission to stay in the UK, such as your right to work, you can share your status easily and securely online by signing in to the ‘view and prove’ service and getting a share code. You then need to give the share code to the person checking your status, as well as your date of birth, which is used as an extra security check when checking your status.

Share codes can only be used for their originally selected purpose. All share codes begin with a letter indicating the purpose. If a share code begins with the letter ‘W’(work), it means the share code was generated by a prospective or existing employee to evidence their right to work. Employers cannot accept or use share codes beginning with the letter ‘R’ (rent) or ‘S’ (general immigration status) as these are meant for other services. The share code is valid for 90 days from the time it is issued and can be used as many times as needed within that period.

You will need an eVisa to demonstrate your permission to travel to the UK. Before travelling internationally, you should:

set up access to your eVisa by creating a UKVI account, if you do not have an account already

make sure your current travel document is linked to your UKVI account

You should keep your expired BRP, if you have one, as it may help with future applications to stay in the UK. You may also want it for your personal records.

Refusal of an asylum claim

If you are refused asylum, we will give you a letter explaining why. The letter will explain whether you have a right of appeal against this decision. If you disagree with the decision and are entitled to appeal, you will also receive information on how to appeal.

Requirement to leave the UK

If your asylum claim is withdrawn or you do not qualify for permission to stay and you are at the end of any appeal process (or if you do not submit an appeal), you will be required to leave the UK. It is expected that you should leave the UK within 21 days. If you do not leave voluntarily, the Home Office will enforce your removal. If your removal is enforced, you will be banned from travelling to the UK for up to 10 years. For further information, see Mandatory refusal period.

Voluntary Returns Service (VRS)

There is support available to you at all stages of the asylum process if you decide that you wish to return home as you no longer want to claim asylum in the United Kingdom. If you decide to make your own arrangements to leave the UK, you should inform the Home Office, and your asylum claim can be withdrawn. You can notify us directly or use the independent support services detailed within this guidance (see section 4 – Getting advice and assistance).

If you have child dependants under 18 years old, you will be asked about their protection needs. Their protection needs may be the same as yours, or they may have additional or different protection needs, or they may have no protection needs.

If a child has the same protection needs as their parent whose claim they are dependent on, the asylum claims of the parent and child may be considered together as a Family asylum claim. Under a Family Asylum Claim we will make a single collective decision based on the information provided by the main claimant. All those being considered as part of the Family asylum claim will be served with their own decision letter, as each person is being treated as having made their own asylum claim. This means that each person may have their own appeal right if refused.

Where your children have additional or different protection needs and are considered to have claimed asylum in their own right, their asylum claim will be individually considered. They will be treated as an accompanied asylum-seeking child claiming in their own right and their case dealt with by decision makers trained in processing children’s asylum cases.

If your children have no protection needs, they can still be a dependant on your claim. This means that they will be considered for a grant of permission to stay in-line with you if your asylum or human rights claim is successful.

For further information, see Dependants and former dependants: caseworker guidance and family asylum claims.

What happens if I have dependants, or I am a dependant of someone else claiming asylum?

Dependants must be registered in person at a screening event. If you are claiming asylum and you want any of your dependants (partner or children under 18 years old) to be part of your asylum claim, then you must bring them with you to your screening appointment so they can be registered at the same time. If you do not do this, you will need to send a request to bring them to another registration event for them to be added before you receive a decision on your claim.

Your request must include the following information and evidence:

your full name, date of birth, and nationality

any reference numbers the Home Office has provided to you

the full name, date of birth, and nationality of your dependant

what your relationship is to the person who you want to include as your dependant

any evidence you have of your relationship to the person who you want to include as a dependant on your claim, for example a UK birth certificate for your UK-born child

Send your request to include a dependant on your asylum application by email or post:

Email: AHROcentralcommunicationshub@contactus.homeoffice.gov.uk

Post:

UKVI PO Box 7782

Village Way

Bilston

WV1 9QB

If they meet the requirements, you’ll be given instructions on how to schedule a screening appointment to register them as a dependant on your asylum claim. See the ‘Your partner and children’ section of Claim Asylum in The UK: Your partner and children – GOV.UK

You cannot add dependants to your claim once you have been granted any form of permission to stay as part of the asylum process, for example, refugee status or humanitarian protection.

If you have children born in the UK after you have been granted refugee status or humanitarian protection and they are not British citizens, you should apply for permission to stay on their behalf.

Unaccompanied asylum-seeking children

Claims from those under 18 years of age are considered under a different process from adult claims, due to the specific needs and requirements of children. We will, when considering claims from children, consider the need to safeguard and promote the welfare of children in the UK.

We will contact your Local Authority’s Children’s Services department on your behalf if you are not already known to them. They will be responsible for looking after you and providing you with accommodation if you are not accompanied by an adult.

If you are an unaccompanied asylum-seeking child (UASC) in England, we will also give your details to the Independent Unaccompanied Asylum Seeking Children Support Service (IUSS), which is run by an independent charity called the Refugee Council, who will advise and assist you in your contact with the Home Office and local authority. In Scotland, the Scottish Guardianship is a statutory service that will provide support to UASCs. In Northern Ireland, the Department of Health will appoint a social worker to act as an independent guardian to assist and support UASCs.

If you are a child claiming asylum in your own right, you must usually complete a Statement of Evidence Form (SEF) to progress your claim, although in a small number of cases you may be included in a different process where this is not required.

For further information, please see our Children’s asylum claims guidance.

Your rights and responsibilities while claiming asylum

If the UK is responsible for considering your claim, your rights and responsibilities whilst you are claiming asylum include:

remaining in the UK throughout the duration of your asylum claim

having the opportunity to give a full account of your reasons for claiming asylum, and having your claim considered fairly and accurately

being assured of confidentiality concerning your asylum claim (the UK will not inform your country of origin that you have made a claim for asylum)

having access to support and accommodation if you are eligible

having legal representation (free legal advice depends on your financial circumstances)

having the right to appeal against your asylum decision if you are eligible

Sexual and gender identity support

For advice, information, and support if you identify as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and/or another minority orientation or gender identity you can contact: Rainbow Migration

Living and working in the United Kingdom

Will I be given permission to work in the UK?

You are generally not allowed to work while your claim for asylum is being considered. However, if you have previously been given valid permission to stay and the right to work in the UK, your ARC will state whether you continue to have work permissions. If your ARC does not state this and you believe it should, you can follow the guidance on GOV.UK.

If we have not made a decision on your initial asylum claim after one year (and this delay is not attributed to you), you may request Permission to Work in certain job roles on Appendix Skilled Occupations at RQF level 6 or above by completing the Permission to work (PTW1) Form.

This right will cease if your claim for asylum is finally determined as unsuccessful and your appeal rights are exhausted.

If your claim was decided and refused within 12 months but you have made an appeal against that decision, you will not be granted permission to work.

For more information on how to apply, see Working while an asylum claim is considered.

Will I be able to undertake any voluntary work?

You may undertake voluntary work whilst your claim is being considered at any stage of the process, and you do not need to apply to the Home Office. Volunteering involves spending time, unpaid, doing something that aims to benefit the environment or someone (individuals or groups). The activity must not amount to unpaid employment or payment in kind (such as you are being given something other than money in exchange for working, including, for example, accommodation). By volunteering for a charity or public sector organisation, you can support your local community, and this will also help your integration if you are granted protection status in the UK.

For more information on volunteering, see Working while an asylum claim is considered.

Criminal and anti-social behaviour

UK laws apply from the moment you arrive in the UK. Breaking the law could result in:

Being arrested by the police

Being sent to prison

Having your asylum claim refused

Being forced to leave the UK

Removal of your asylum support.

Criminal and/or anti-social behaviour is not tolerated in the UK. Action may be taken against you if you are found taking part in:

violent, aggressive, or abusive behaviour

possessing, using, or selling drugs

carrying, using, or threatening to use offensive weapons

rowdy, nuisance, or intimidating behaviour

vandalism or graffiti

begging, fighting, spitting or anti-social drinking.

The UK is a diverse country. People of all backgrounds, beliefs, genders, and sexualities live here. Different religions are practised openly. Same-sex relationships are legal. Under UK law, everyone is equal. You must treat everyone with dignity and respect.

In the UK, men and women are equal. This is protected by law. Violence and abusive behaviour, especially against women and children, is illegal at all times, whether in public, in private, or at home. This applies to behaviour towards partners, former partners, family members, friends, or strangers. There are no exceptions. This includes:

Touching someone without their permission in a way which is considered sexual because of what is done or the circumstances

Harassing or abusing someone in person or online

Grooming a child in person or online

Exposing your genitals in public

Taking, sharing, or threatening to share private or intimate photos of someone without their permission

Stalking someone (repeatedly following, contacting, watching, or interfering with them)

Sending repeated unwanted messages or making repeated unwanted calls

Behaviour that makes someone feel scared or unsafe

Physically hurting someone

Controlling someone’s behaviour, money, clothing, relationships, or how they live their life (including what they wear and who they see or speak to)

The UK has strict laws about sexual consent.

People must clearly agree to have sex or take part in any type of sexual activity. This agreement must be freely given, without pressure or persuasion. This is called consent. Sex without consent is rape, which is a very serious crime in the UK.

You must never pressure or force someone to have sex. You must never continue if someone says no or seems unsure. If you are not sure they want to, you must stop. You must never assume silence means yes. Silence is not consent.

You must not have sex with someone who is asleep, unconscious, or too affected by alcohol or drugs to agree. You must not give someone alcohol or drugs to make them have sex.

You must not change what someone agreed to (for example, removing a condom) without their permission.

You must not lie or mislead someone in order to have sex with them.

It is illegal to pressure someone to have sex or engage in sexual activity in return for money, gifts, housing, or favours.

Sex, sexual activity, or sexual touching with anyone under the age of 16 is illegal, even if they say they agree to it.

It is also illegal for anyone under the age of 18 to get married and to force someone to get married through pressure, including physical, psychological, or emotional abuse. This applies regardless of what is legal or accepted in your home country.

Any of these behaviours could result in:

Being arrested by the police

Being sent to prison

Having your asylum claim refused

Being forced to leave the UK.

Removal of your asylum support
